name: Ruxolitinib oral

lead: Oral ruxolitinib (Jakafi) is a prescription JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor approved for myelofibrosis, polycythemia vera and graft-versus-host disease. People with alopecia areata follow it as an off-label route to hair regrowth.

By blocking cytokine signalling in immune cells it is thought to ease the immune attack on follicles. Alopecia areata is listed as an area of investigation; other JAK inhibitors have approvals or trial data in that condition.

paras: It is a daily pill prescribed and monitored by a physician for its approved conditions; use for hair is off-label.

Reported effects include low blood counts, infections including shingles, and raised cholesterol and liver enzymes. Reviews discuss cancer and infection concerns for the JAK inhibitor class. Prescription only.

angle.text: Oral ruxolitinib blocks JAK1 and JAK2 signalling, which is thought to ease the immune attack on follicles in alopecia areata and allow regrowth. It is approved for blood and transplant conditions, and hair use is off-label.

lead: Oral ruxolitinib, sold as Jakafi in the United States and Jakavi elsewhere, is a prescription Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor that blocks JAK1 and JAK2. It is approved for myelofibrosis, polycythemia vera and graft-versus-host disease, and it appears in hair-loss discussion because the same JAK-STAT signalling pathway is implicated in alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks hair follicles.[1][2][3]

The route from this drug to appearance is through the immune system: dampening JAK signalling in the follicle region is the mechanism by which JAK inhibitors as a class have been used to let hair regrow in alopecia areata. Other JAK inhibitors, not ruxolitinib, hold the approvals for that condition: baricitinib (June 2022), ritlecitinib (June 2023) and deuruxolitinib (July 2024).[4] Wikipedia lists alopecia areata among ruxolitinib's investigated uses, but its approved indications are blood and transplant conditions.[1]

The research base for oral ruxolitinib consists of registered trials in haematologic malignancies, myelofibrosis, graft-versus-host disease and COVID-19, and reviews of JAK inhibitor safety in dermatology; no trial results for oral ruxolitinib in alopecia areata have been published.

paras: The FDA approved oral ruxolitinib in November 2011 for intermediate- or high-risk myelofibrosis on the basis of the COMFORT-I and COMFORT-II phase III trials, which were reported in March 2012 and showed reduced spleen size and relief of symptoms. The European Union approved it in 2012.[1]

Later US approvals were for polycythemia vera in people who responded poorly to or could not tolerate hydroxyurea (2014, RESPONSE trial), steroid-refractory acute graft-versus-host disease (May 2019) and chronic graft-versus-host disease in patients aged 12 and older (September 2021).[1] It is classed as an orphan drug and is prescription-only in the US, UK, Canada, Australia and the EU.[1]

Alopecia areata is listed among the investigated uses of ruxolitinib in Wikipedia's article, along with plaque psoriasis and some lymphomas.[1] The JAK-STAT pathway is central to several immune-mediated skin diseases, including atopic dermatitis, as an updated review describes.[2]

Within the class, an early signal came from a 2014 news report of a man with complete hair loss who regrew hair on tofacitinib, an arthritis drug, and a 2015 Science Advances study reported that blocking JAK-STAT signalling promotes hair growth.[4] Baricitinib (Olumiant) became the first systemic treatment approved for severe alopecia areata in June 2022, followed by ritlecitinib (Litfulo) in June 2023 and deuruxolitinib (Leqselvi) in July 2024.[4]

The topical cream form, Opzelura, is a separate product: the FDA approved it for mild to moderate atopic dermatitis in September 2021 and for vitiligo in July 2022, described as the first approved treatment for repigmentation in vitiligo.[1]

The pivotal evidence for oral ruxolitinib comes from the COMFORT trials in myelofibrosis,[1] and a phase III registered trial of INC424 for myelofibrosis enrolled 2,233 participants.[5] A phase II registered study of ruxolitinib in steroid-refractory graft-versus-host disease enrolled 75 patients.[6] No trial results for oral ruxolitinib in alopecia areata were located; the evidence for hair regrowth with JAK inhibitors rests on other agents in the class.[4]

A 2023 retrospective cohort of 49 children with beta-thalassemia major reviewed adding ruxolitinib to graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis after stem cell transplantation.[7] A 2026 retrospective analysis looked at topical ruxolitinib with or without oral baricitinib in active non-segmental vitiligo.[8]

In its approved indications, reported effects include low platelet, red cell and neutrophil counts, urinary tract infections, bleeding and bruising, weight gain, raised cholesterol, dizziness, headache and elevated liver enzymes. In polycythemia vera, high triglycerides and high blood pressure have also been reported.[1] Herpes zoster and case reports of opportunistic infections appear, and viral infections such as herpes zoster may replicate more readily during treatment.[1]

Class-wide concerns are discussed in dermatology. A 2024 narrative review examined cancer risk with biologics and JAK inhibitors, noting concerns about malignancy and opportunistic infection.[9] The FDA requires a boxed warning for tofacitinib, baricitinib and upadacitinib covering serious heart events, cancer, blood clots and death, and the European Medicines Agency recommends using certain JAK inhibitors in older people, smokers and those at high cardiovascular or cancer risk only when no suitable alternative exists.[4] A 2025 retrospective TriNetX cohort compared the systemic risk profiles of topical ruxolitinib, oral JAK inhibitors and conventional topical therapy in atopic dermatitis, after the FDA issued a boxed warning for the topical product assuming risks similar to oral agents.[10]

Ruxolitinib selectively inhibits JAK1 and JAK2. Normally these enzymes activate STAT proteins at cytokine receptors, changing gene expression; the drug suppresses the overactive JAK signalling seen in myelofibrosis.[1]

Oral bioavailability is about 95 percent and plasma protein binding about 97 percent. It is metabolised mainly by CYP3A4 in the liver, and the elimination half-life is roughly 3 hours. About 74 percent is excreted in urine and 22 percent in faeces.[1]

Incyte developed ruxolitinib, which is also known by the research codes INCB018424 and INC424, and markets it as Jakafi in the United States; Novartis sells it elsewhere as Jakavi.[1] An early phase II registered study, started in 2008, enrolled 51 patients with advanced haematologic malignancies.[11] A phase III pancreatic cancer trial was stopped in February 2016 for insufficient efficacy.[1]

Registered studies span graft-versus-host disease in adults and children, T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukaemia and COVID-19 cytokine storm.[12][13] A 2025 expanded-access report described emergency use of ruxolitinib in COVID-19-associated cytokine storm.[14] Wikipedia also lists plaque psoriasis, alopecia areata and several lymphomas among investigated uses, and notes an animal study in aged mice in which eight weeks of treatment reduced senescent-cell interference with fat cell formation.[1]

No studies exist for oral ruxolitinib in alopecia areata; Wikipedia describes that use as under investigation, without results.[1] Registered trials of oral ruxolitinib concern haematologic malignancies, myelofibrosis, graft-versus-host disease and COVID-19.[11][5][6][13] The COMFORT-I and COMFORT-II phase III trials supported the 2011 myelofibrosis approval.[1]

timeline.event: FDA approves oral ruxolitinib for myelofibrosis.[1]
European Union approval; COMFORT trial results reported.[1]
Approval for steroid-refractory acute graft-versus-host disease.[1]
Chronic graft-versus-host disease approval; topical ruxolitinib approved for atopic dermatitis.[1]
Opzelura approved for vitiligo; baricitinib becomes the first systemic treatment approved for severe alopecia areata.[1][4]
Ritlecitinib approved for severe alopecia areata.[4]
